Distribution-preserving surrogates: emulate, invert, check

Source: vignettes/surrogate-workflow.Rmd
surrogate-workflow.Rmd

Why

Does the fast stand-in I trained for my simulator actually preserve the simulator’s predictive distribution, not just its mean, and would I be able to tell if it did not? That is the question anyone plugging a surrogate into a mechanism lens has to answer before trusting it, and it is what this vignette exists to answer: a surrogate (or emulator) that reports a predictive distribution, not a point, walked through the whole loop – ingest, fit, read, invert, check – so the distribution can be inspected and falsified rather than assumed. The reference surrogate ships with quorum itself and needs no other package, so every code chunk below runs as shown; one chunk needs kernR and is guarded accordingly.

What

fb_ensemble() carries a simulation ensemble (contract C5) – a design matrix paired with the simulator’s row-aligned response, from whatever producer built it. fit_surrogate() trains a fast, distribution-preserving stand-in for the simulator (contract C7): its predict() method returns a mean and a standard deviation for every output, so a downstream step never has to treat the surrogate as exact. fb_surrogate_ies() is the calibration consumer – an Ensemble Smoother with Multiple Data Assimilation that inverts observed data against the surrogate in place of the simulator. fb_surrogate_ppc() is the predictive check – a maximum-mean-discrepancy test, run through kernR, of whether the surrogate’s own predictive draws are distinguishable from the true simulator’s outputs. fb_cov_slice() reads one row’s cross-output covariance out of a joint prediction.

Do

A simulator we can check against

We use a linear forward model y = G theta so the truth is known and the inversion is exact in expectation. Three outputs, two parameters, and a little observation noise.

g <- rbind(c(1.5, -0.8), c(0.4, 1.1), c(-0.9, 0.6)) # 3 outputs x 2 params
n_train <- 300L
theta <- cbind(
  p1 = runif(n_train, -3, 3),
  p2 = runif(n_train, -3, 3)
)
y <- theta %*% t(g) + matrix(rnorm(n_train * 3L, 0, 0.1), n_train, 3L)
colnames(y) <- c("o1", "o2", "o3")

The ensemble is ingested through the C5 contract, so any conforming producer (a PESTO manifest, a raw apsimx run, a saved file) feeds a surrogate the same way. Here we build one directly from the design and the outputs.

ens <- fb_ensemble(
  params = as.data.frame(theta),
  outputs = as.data.frame(y),
  provenance = list(source = "raw")
)
ens
#> -- fb_ensemble (simulation ensemble, contract C5) ----------
#>   source : raw
#>   sets   : 300
#>   params : 2 (p1, p2)
#>   outputs: 3
#>   labelled: FALSE | observed: FALSE
#> ------------------------------------------------------------

Fit a surrogate and read its distribution

fit_surrogate() trains the emulator. The default reference method, "rff", is a random-Fourier-features Bayesian linear model whose predictive variance is set by evidence maximisation, so the reported standard deviation is calibrated rather than an arbitrary ridge.

sur <- fit_surrogate(ens)
sur
#> -- fb_surrogate (distribution-preserving emulator, C7) -----
#>   method : rff | train sets: 300
#>   params : 2 (p1, p2)
#>   outputs: 3 (o1, o2, o3)
#>   rff fit: joint (cross-output covariance) | ARD
#>   predict(): per-output <name>_mean + <name>_sd (cov = TRUE for joint)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------

predict() returns, for each emulated output <o>, a <o>_mean and a <o>_sd column. The standard deviation is the distribution-preserving part of the contract.

newdata <- data.frame(p1 = c(1.0, -2.0), p2 = c(0.5, 1.5))
pred_new <- predict(sur, newdata)
Predictive mean and SD at the two rows of newdata.
o1_mean o1_sd o2_mean o2_sd o3_mean o3_sd
1.266 0.343 0.942 0.235 -0.712 0.229
-4.137 0.344 0.936 0.236 2.640 0.229 
p1_sweep <- seq(-3, 6, length.out = 200L)
sweep_df <- data.frame(p1 = p1_sweep, p2 = 0)
pred_sweep <- predict(sur, sweep_df)
truth_sweep <- g[1L, 1L] * p1_sweep + g[1L, 2L] * 0
plot(p1_sweep, pred_sweep$o1_mean, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     ylim = range(c(pred_sweep$o1_mean + 2 * pred_sweep$o1_sd,
                    pred_sweep$o1_mean - 2 * pred_sweep$o1_sd, truth_sweep)),
     xlab = "p1 (p2 fixed at 0)", ylab = "o1", main = "Predictive band vs truth")
polygon(c(p1_sweep, rev(p1_sweep)),
        c(pred_sweep$o1_mean + 2 * pred_sweep$o1_sd,
          rev(pred_sweep$o1_mean - 2 * pred_sweep$o1_sd)),
        col = grDevices::adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.2), border = NA)
lines(p1_sweep, truth_sweep, lty = 2, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
rect(-3, par("usr")[3], 3, par("usr")[4],
     col = grDevices::adjustcolor("grey50", alpha.f = 0.08), border = NA)
legend("topleft", c("predictive mean", "truth", "design range"),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick", "grey50"), lty = c(1, 2, NA),
       pch = c(NA, NA, 15), lwd = c(2, 2, NA), bty = "n")

Predictive mean (line) and +/- 2 standard-deviation band (ribbon) for output o1 as p1 sweeps from -3 to 6 at p2 = 0, against the true linear response (dashed); the design only covers p1 in [-3, 3] (shaded), so the region to the right of it is genuinely out-of-design.

Inside the shaded design range the band hugs the truth and stays tight; once p1 moves past 3 the mean starts to bend away from the true straight line and the band widens accordingly – the reference surrogate is genuinely less certain where it has never seen data, which is the behaviour clause 2 of the C7 contract exists to require of every registered conformer.

pred_train <- predict(sur, as.data.frame(theta))
fit_df <- data.frame(
  observed = y[, "o1"], predicted = pred_train$o1_mean, sd = pred_train$o1_sd
)
ggplot2::ggplot(
  fit_df, ggplot2::aes(x = observed, y = predicted, colour = sd)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50",
                       linetype = 2) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "predictive SD") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "ensemble output o1 (training)", y = "surrogate predicted mean o1",
    title = "The surrogate against the ensemble it emulates"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

The surrogate’s predicted mean against the ensemble’s own training outputs for o1, one point per training draw, coloured by the surrogate’s reported predictive SD at that point; the dashed line is exact recovery. A well-fitted surrogate on an easy, near-linear response like this one sits tight on the line with a narrow, roughly constant SD range.

By default the reference surrogate fits the outputs jointly, so it preserves the cross-output predictive covariance, not only the per-output marginals. predict(..., cov = TRUE) returns that covariance as a per-row array, and fb_cov_slice() reads one row’s k-by-k slice.

pc <- predict(sur, newdata, cov = TRUE)
cov_slice_1 <- fb_cov_slice(pc, 1L)
Predictive cross-output covariance for row 1 of newdata.
o1 o2 o3
o1 0.118 -0.001 -0.066
o2 -0.001 0.055 0.005
o3 -0.066 0.005 0.052 
cov_dense <- fb_cov_slice(pc, 1L)
sur_lr_fig <- fit_surrogate(ens, cov_rank = 1L)
pc_lr <- predict(sur_lr_fig, newdata, cov = "lowrank")
u <- pc_lr$cov_lowrank$u; d <- pc_lr$cov_lowrank$d; infl <- pc_lr$cov_lowrank$infl[1L]
cov_lr <- infl * (u %*% t(u) + diag(d))
zlim <- range(c(cov_dense, cov_lr))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))
image(cov_dense, main = "dense", axes = FALSE, zlim = zlim, col = heat.colors(20))
image(cov_lr, main = "rank-1", axes = FALSE, zlim = zlim, col = heat.colors(20))

Predictive cross-output covariance for row 1 of newdata (dense k x k slice, left) beside its rank-1 low-rank reconstruction (right); darker cells are larger covariance magnitude. 

par(op)

The rank-1 reconstruction reproduces the diagonal of the dense covariance exactly (clause 5 of the C7 contract) and visibly recovers the same off-diagonal pattern from a single latent factor, at O(k) rather than O(k^2) storage – the picture that makes the low-rank approximation’s fidelity, not just its numeric closeness, inspectable. The diagonal of that slice equals the <o>_sd values squared, exactly – the marginal contract is never broken by the joint fit.

Invert: recover parameters from data

fb_surrogate_ies() is the calibration consumer. It runs an Ensemble Smoother with Multiple Data Assimilation (ES-MDA), driving a prior parameter ensemble toward agreement with observed data using only the surrogate in place of the simulator. Because the surrogate is distribution-preserving, its predictive variance is folded into the data covariance, so emulator uncertainty inflates the assimilation noise where the emulator is least sure.

theta_true <- c(p1 = 1.2, p2 = -0.7)
observed <- as.numeric(g %*% theta_true)
names(observed) <- c("o1", "o2", "o3")

prior <- data.frame(
  p1 = rnorm(300, 0, 1.5),
  p2 = rnorm(300, 0, 1.5)
)
fit <- fb_surrogate_ies(sur, observed, obs_sd = 0.05, prior = prior, seed = 7)
fit
#> -- fb_surrogate_ies (surrogate-accelerated ES-MDA, C7 consumer) -
#>   surrogate: rff | iters: 4 | realisations: 300
#>   data misfit:  6830 -> 147.7
#>   parameter  prior_mean posterior_mean
#> 1        p1  0.07365159      1.1578499
#> 2        p2 -0.10138003     -0.6978132
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------

The posterior ensemble concentrates near the truth, and the data misfit falls from prior to posterior.

recovery_tab <- rbind(
  truth = theta_true,
  prior_mean = colMeans(prior),
  posterior_mean = colMeans(fit$posterior)
)
Truth, prior mean and posterior mean after ES-MDA.
p1 p2
truth 1.200 -0.700
prior_mean 0.074 -0.101
posterior_mean 1.158 -0.698 
plot(seq_along(fit$misfit) - 1L, fit$misfit, type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "steelblue", xlab = "ES-MDA iteration", ylab = "mean data misfit",
     main = "Inversion trace")

Mean data misfit across the ES-MDA iterations, from the prior ensemble (iteration 0) to the final posterior.

The misfit falls monotonically from the prior to the final iteration, which is the diagnostic that the assimilation is actually pulling the ensemble toward agreement with the observed data rather than merely inflating its spread.

Check: did the surrogate distort the distribution?

A surrogate can recover the mean while getting the spread or the cross-output correlation wrong. fb_surrogate_ppc() tests the predictive distribution itself, by drawing from the surrogate at held-out parameter sets and comparing the draw cloud to the true simulator outputs with kernR’s maximum-mean-discrepancy posterior-predictive check. The MMD test lives in kernR – quorum only generates the predictive sample – so this chunk runs only when kernR is installed.

set.seed(4)
held <- data.frame(p1 = runif(60, -2.5, 2.5), p2 = runif(60, -2.5, 2.5))
truth_held <- held$p1 %o% g[, 1] + held$p2 %o% g[, 2] +
  matrix(rnorm(60 * 3L, 0, 0.1), 60, 3L)
colnames(truth_held) <- c("o1", "o2", "o3")

check <- fb_surrogate_ppc(
  sur, held, as.data.frame(truth_held),
  n_draws = 5L, seed = 1L, n_permutations = 199L
)
c(p_value = check$p_value, reject = check$reject)
#> p_value  reject 
#>       1       0

A high p-value (no rejection) means the surrogate’s predictive draws are indistinguishable from the simulator’s outputs – the distribution was preserved, not merely the mean. The check is joint by default, so it exercises the cross-output correlation, not only each output’s spread.

Many outputs: a low-rank covariance

When a simulator has a large number of outputs whose covariance is driven by a few latent factors, the dense k-by-k covariance is wasteful. cov_rank = q stores the cross-output covariance in a rank-q factor-analysis form, reducing the storage from order k squared to order k times q, while reproducing the covariance diagonal – and hence every <o>_sd – exactly.

sur_lr <- fit_surrogate(ens, cov_rank = 1L)
sur_lr$fit$sigma_lr$rank
#> [1] 1

Both consumers use the factored form natively, so the dense covariance is never formed: fb_surrogate_ies() folds it into the Kalman update through the Woodbury identity, and fb_surrogate_ppc() samples it factored (and, with project = TRUE, runs the discrepancy test in the q-dimensional factor space, which is cheaper and higher-powered on the correlated structure for a large output count). The factor itself is fitted by one of three methods: an eigen-truncation (the default), a factor-analysis EM (cov_method = "fa", more faithful when the residual noise is uneven across outputs), or "auto" (picks between them by the heteroscedasticity of the eigen-residual diagonal).

Read

The training-fit figure above recovers the ensemble’s own outputs with correlation 0.994 and every predictive SD in a narrow band, which is what a near-linear response fitted well should look like; a wide spread of SDs, or points that stray far from the dashed line at a narrow SD, would say the surrogate is confidently wrong rather than genuinely uncertain. The inversion recovers p1 and p2 to within 0.042 of the truth, and the misfit trace falls from 6830.346 at the prior to 147.701 at the final iteration – a 97.8% reduction. The rank-1 covariance reconstruction reproduces the dense diagonal to machine precision, which is the exactness clause 5 of the C7 contract requires and not merely a visual approximation.

Limits

This is a linear forward model, chosen so the inversion is exact in expectation and every number above has a known truth to check against; a stiff or sharply nonlinear simulator would show the reference surrogate’s band widening faster and its inversion converging less cleanly. The predictive check needs kernR and is skipped without it, in which case the distortion question this vignette asks is left open rather than answered either way. The reference rff surrogate keeps quorum standalone-functional, but it is deliberately simple: richer emulators – a Gaussian process, kernR’s conditional mean embedding – register through register_surrogate() and are consumed through exactly the same predict() contract, so the inversion and the check above work unchanged with a sibling’s surrogate in place of the reference, and a richer registered emulator will preserve the distribution where this reference cannot on a harder problem. A surrogate is only as trustworthy as its predictive distribution, which is why the standard deviation is a contract requirement rather than an optional extra, and why the inversion and the predictive check ship alongside the emulator instead of being left to a downstream user to improvise.

What to read next

Getting started with quorum is the shorter path through the same seam, alongside the ensemble on-ramp and the koine fourth opinion. A quorum of lenses on Study A0 and Adding a lens pick up past this vignette’s stopping point: turning an ingested, emulated estimate into a lens and comparing it against another.

Reproduce

Seed 1 set in this vignette’s setup chunk; set.seed(4) before the predictive check and seed = 7 passed to fb_surrogate_ies() for the inversion. Package versions follow.
